newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine, Belarus sign border pact, debt still snag.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine, Belarus sign border pact, debt still snag.

text.p: The presidents of Ukraine and Belarus signed pacts formally defining the 1,200-km (800-mile) border between the two former Soviet republics on Monday but failed to resolve the issue of Ukraine's debt to its northern neighbour.

"Twelve hundred km without firing a shot -- we are coming closer together," President Leonid Kuchma told a news conference after signing three border accords with Belarus's Alexander Lukashenko in the Ukrainian capital, Kiev.
"Borders do not exist to separate peoples," said Lukashenko, who signed a union treaty with Russia last month and has called for all three Slav former Soviet states to reunite.

Kiev, whose relations with Moscow have been distinctly chilly, has initiated a similar border-delimiting process with Russia. But Moscow has cited lack of cash for the work as a reason for slow progress in talks with Ukraine.

Conscious of difficulties in its relations with Moscow, Ukraine has strived to maintain good relations with Minsk and is concerned that Lukashenko's union treaty could mean Russian control of Belarus's population of 10 million.
Lukashenko, who is due to sign a detailed annexe to the treaty with Russian President Boris Yeltsin on May 23, said last week Moscow was not yet ready to create a single state.
In Kiev on Monday he said there would be "an interstate union, formed by two sovereign, independent states".
Lukashenko added that Moscow and Minsk had resolved four of six differences over the union's charter and the remaining ones would be sorted out at the highest level. He did not elaborate.

Lukashenko also criticised the Russian media, sections of which are sympathetic to liberal opponents of the union, for "too much fuss" around the treaty. Russian liberals fear linking with Lukashenko's authoritarian politics and Soviet-style economics could harm Russia's post-communist reforms.
Kuchma earlier this year criticised the Russian-Belarussian union, saying it could destroy the 12-member Commonwealth of Independent States grouping most former Soviet republics.
But while hosting Lukashenko he took a softer stance.
"This is the right of the Belarussian and Russian people to form some sort of union," Kuchma said. "We, as neighbours, must respect this right."

Nine other economic agreements were signed at the start of Lukashenko's two-day visit to Ukraine. But government sources said there was no deal on how and when Kiev would pay its $217 million debt to Minsk.
More than a hundred members of Ukraine's Rukh nationalist party, which has supported Lukashenko's anti-union opponents, staged a demonstration criticising his treaty with Russia.
Both leaders also discussed NATO's plans to invite some east European countries to join the Western defence alliance.
Russia and Belarus both fiercely oppose the move while Ukraine does not. "We really do have different views, different approaches towards relations with NATO," Lukashenko said.
